rows.evidence: Q1: Section 5.3 Results, Cases 1-5 and Figures 3-8 - the authors report their own model runs of a linear-quadratic optimal control scheme coupled to a lumped soil-crop-climate state space model, producing hourly irrigation rates over a 50-day horizon for maize on Panoche clay, with water balances (e.g., Case 1 low-cost: 48 cm applied, 30 cm drained; high-cost: 16 cm applied, 2 cm percolation).
rows.notes: The study is a pure simulation/optimisation exercise. Its outputs (optimal irrigation sequences, cumulative fluxes, water storage) are never compared with measurements from any real irrigated field; the authors state that the examples test the correct behaviour of the controller and that results follow a priori expected patterns, and that the model is a conceptualisation subject to revision. The reference to past field experiments calibrating the crop model concerns earlier work (Protopapas and Bras 1988), not this study. Hence under the rule that a model run never checked against observations is not own evidence, Q2 is no for water conservation. Note the passage says 'daily' rates whereas the study optimises hourly rates; and the paper restricts itself to the deterministic case (no climatic uncertainty) and reports CPU time and iteration counts but no dispersion measures.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 5.3 Results, Cases 2-5 and Figures 5-8 - own model runs in which the controller is given saline initial soil and/or saline irrigation water (1000-3000 mg/L) and the optimal sequence stabilises or leaches root-zone salinity (e.g., Case 3: salt-free water leaches 3000 mg/L salts within the first 20 days; Case 4: high rates hold salinity at 1000 mg/L).
rows.notes: The salinity results are simulated outputs of a lumped mass-balance salt model under optimal control; no root-zone salinity measurements from a real field are compared with the model output, so the study provides no own empirical evidence that app-based scheduling minimises salinity or improves soil health. The authors themselves describe the results as a priori expected patterns and a demonstration of controller behaviour, and acknowledge the model cannot account for inaccurate representation of system dynamics. Q2 therefore no; downstream questions not applicable.

notes: Full text available including appendix. The paper is a methodological optimal-control/simulation study (deterministic case, maize, Panoche clay, 50-day horizon, hourly time step). It reports model runs but no field validation of the irrigation schedules or their water-saving and salinity outcomes, so it is scored as primary (Q1 yes) but without own evidence on the claimed effects (Q2 no) for both rows.
